# Vectorbreak

> AI red-team audits, training, and custom defensive engineering for agentic and RAG-enabled systems. The Five Surfaces methodology — 5 attack surfaces, 69 risk classes, 8 published case studies.

Vectorbreak helps teams shipping AI agents, RAG pipelines, and LLM-integrated products find and fix security problems before production incidents. Founded 2026. Solo-authored methodology and case studies.

## Core

- [Homepage](https://vectorbreak.com): Product positioning, services, and methodology overview
- [Five Surfaces Methodology](https://vectorbreak.com#methodology): The canonical threat model covering model, context, retrieval, tools/MCP, and runtime

## Services

- [Audit](https://vectorbreak.com#pricing): Fixed-fee red-team engagements from $4.5k (Pulse) to $285k (Annual Program)
- [Training & Education](https://vectorbreak.com#services): Two-day Five Surfaces workshop with hands-on labs
- [Custom Build](https://vectorbreak.com#services): Defensive tooling, MCP hardening, prompt-injection monitoring, agent-loop circuit breakers
- [Community](https://vectorbreak.com#community): Vetted Discord for practitioners — weekly threat-class drops, live PoC reviews, monthly threat-intel briefing

## Methodology

- [Five Surfaces Overview](https://vectorbreak.com#methodology): 5 surfaces, 69 risk classes, OWASP-ASI + MITRE-ATLAS mapped
- [Surface 1: Input/Output](https://vectorbreak.com#methodology): Direct prompts, jailbreaks, output sanitization, multi-modal injection (13 classes)
- [Surface 2: Retrieval](https://vectorbreak.com#methodology): RAG corpora, indexers, indirect injection, knowledge-base poisoning (11 classes)
- [Surface 3: Tool-call/MCP](https://vectorbreak.com#methodology): Function calling, MCP servers, tool poisoning, privilege escalation (20 classes)
- [Surface 4: Model](https://vectorbreak.com#methodology): Weights, adapter chains, system prompts, training-data extraction (11 classes)
- [Surface 5: Runtime](https://vectorbreak.com#methodology): Sandbox escape, prompt-to-RCE, agent loops, memory persistence (14 classes)

> Source: https://vectorbreak.com

## Red-team your AI agent before someone else does.

Productized red-teaming, defensive engineering, and training for agentic and RAG-enabled AI systems. The artifact your cyber-insurance carrier, EU AI Act conformity assessor, and acquirer's diligence team are now asking for.

### The Methodology by the Numbers

**Five surfaces. Sixty-nine risk classes. Eight published case studies. Solo-authored.**

- 5 Attack surfaces
- 69 Risk classes
- 8 Public case studies
- 139 Unit tests, all green

### Five Surfaces: Five Places Production Incidents Live

LLM application security used to be one surface: a chatbot's input box. In 2026 it's five — and four of them are where the production incidents live. OWASP-ASI + MITRE-ATLAS + OWASP-LLM-Top-10 mapped. MIT-licensed.

#### Surface 1: Input / Output (13 classes)

Direct prompts, structured outputs, jailbreaks, sanitization gaps.

The control plane between the operator and the model. Best-understood surface; still where most teams have unaddressed gaps. Tests include direct prompt injection, conversation-history manipulation, structured-output schema injection, universal jailbreak coverage, multi-turn drift, refusal mining, HTML/markdown rendering attacks, code-block escape, and multi-modal input (image, audio, document parsing).

#### Surface 2: Retrieval (11 classes)

RAG corpora, indexers, indirect injection, knowledge-base poisoning.

Everything you put into the prompt — system instructions, retrieved documents, prior turns, tool outputs. This is the dirtiest surface. If anything in your context window came from anywhere a user can influence, you have a prompt-injection problem and you need to know exactly where the trust boundary sits.

#### Surface 3: Tool-Call / MCP (20 classes — most-exploited)

Function calling, MCP servers, tool poisoning, privilege escalation.

The action plane. This is where 2026's highest-severity findings are landing. MCP servers are unsigned code with privileged access to the model's context window. Tests cover tool poisoning (malicious descriptions, adversarial servers, supply-chain compromise, parameter shadowing), cross-server privilege escalation (read-only feeding write-capable, tool-call chains with credential bleed, sub-agent escalation), and confused-deputy patterns.

#### Surface 4: Model (11 classes)

Weights, adapter chains, system prompts, training-data extraction.

The base model itself — its training data, jailbreaks, refusal behavior, alignment drift over context length, behavior under adversarial prompting. Most teams treat this as "the vendor's problem." It isn't, the moment you ship it to a user.

#### Surface 5: Runtime (14 classes)

Sandbox escape, prompt-to-RCE, agent loops, memory persistence.

Where does the model's execution live? Whose authority is it acting under? Hidden loops in agent orchestration that create opportunities for infinite recursion, token bleed, and lateral movement between sessions.

# Page: Five Surfaces Methodology

> Source: https://vectorbreak.com#methodology

The Five Surfaces framework organizes LLM-application security into five distinct attack surfaces, each with its own threat model, test cases, and remediation patterns.

## Surface 1: Input / Output

The control plane between the operator and the model.

**13 risk classes** covering direct prompts, structured outputs, jailbreaks, and sanitization gaps.

### Direct Prompt Injection (FS1-DPI)

- Override of system prompt via user input: Classic "ignore previous instructions" family, authority impersonation, translation pivot, role-play sandwich, multi-modal variations.
- Conversation-history manipulation: Fake assistant messages if history is user-controlled.
- Structured-output schema injection: Can the user influence JSON schema or parsers?

### Jailbreak (FS1-JB)

- Universal jailbreak coverage: Run a battery of published jailbreaks; catalogue what the system blocks vs. allows.
- Multi-turn drift: Guardrails often decay across conversation turns.
- Refusal mining: What does the model refuse? Refusal text often leaks system-prompt language or training details.

### Output Sanitization (FS1-OS)

- HTML/markdown rendering attacks: XSS via script tags, image referer exfil, markdown injection.
- Code-block escape: In IDEs and dev tools, can output break out of code-suggestion context?
- Structured-output escape: Can the model produce malformed JSON that confuses downstream parsers?

### Multi-Modal Input (FS1-MM)

- Image prompt injection: Text in images (visible or steganographic), metadata injection.
- Audio/voice transcription injection: Adversarial audio transcribed as text.
- Document parsing injection: Hidden text in PDFs, comments, form fields.

### History Serialization (FS1-HS)

- Cross-session contamination: Can user A see remnants of user B's session? Do summarizations leak secrets?

## Surface 2: Retrieval

Everything you put into the prompt — system instructions, retrieved documents, prior turns, tool outputs.

**11 risk classes** covering RAG corpora, indexers, indirect injection, and knowledge-base poisoning.

This is the dirtiest surface. If anything in your context window came from anywhere a user can influence, you have a prompt-injection problem and you need to know exactly where the trust boundary sits. Test retrieval source controls, document parsing for injection payloads, embedding-space poisoning, index corruption, and retrieval-result sanitization.

## Surface 3: Tool-Call / MCP

The action plane. This is where 2026's highest-severity findings are landing.

**20 risk classes** covering function calling, MCP servers, tool poisoning, and privilege escalation. Most-exploited surface.

### Tool Poisoning (FS3-TP)

- Malicious tool description injection: MCP servers often populate descriptions dynamically. Can an attacker inject instructions into descriptions that the model treats as authoritative?
- Adversarial MCP server in multi-server config: Can a low-trust server hijack a high-trust server's invocation pattern?
- Skill/plugin marketplace supply chain: Are skills cryptographically signed? Is there manifest review? Disclosure pathway? OpenClaw incident (January 2026) — 824 malicious skills shipped before detection.
- Function schema parameter shadowing: Can the model confuse overlapping parameter names between tools?

### Cross-Server / Cross-Tool Privilege Escalation (FS3-XPE)

- Read-only tool feeds write-capable tool: Can output from a read-only tool (web_fetch, read_file) flow into write-capable tool parameters without re-confirmation?
- Tool-call chain with credential bleed: If a tool result includes a credential in an error path, does it leak into the next tool's parameters?
- Sub-agent escalation: In multi-agent systems, can the parent be tricked into spawning a child with permissions exceeding what was authorized?

### Confused-Deputy Patterns (FS3-CD)

- Identity confusion between MCP server and model: Whose authority is the call executing under?
- OAuth / credential leakage across agent-call chains: Tokens leaked when one tool's result feeds another.

## Surface 4: Model

The base model itself — its training data, jailbreaks, refusal behavior, alignment drift over context length, behavior under adversarial prompting.

**11 risk classes** covering weights, adapter chains, system prompts, and training-data extraction.

Most teams treat this as "the vendor's problem." It isn't, the moment you ship it to a user. Tests cover model watermarking, extraction attacks, fine-tuning backdoors, and in-context behavior under extreme scenarios.

## Surface 5: Runtime

Where does the model's execution live? Whose authority is it acting under?

**14 risk classes** covering sandbox escape, prompt-to-RCE, agent loops, and memory persistence.

Hidden loops in agent orchestration create opportunities for infinite recursion, token bleed, and lateral movement between sessions. Test memory isolation, loop detection, output sinks, and recovery mechanisms.

# Page: Public Case Studies

> Source: https://vectorbreak.com#receipts

## Methodology Validated Against Named Targets

Eight published assessments. Six PASS verdicts on Claude-family hosts. Two FAIL verdicts on cross-family direct-to-model targets — the empirical property that auditors, insurers, and acquirers need to see before they accept a methodology as evidence-grade.

| # | Target | Surface Scope | Findings | Verdict |
|---|--------|---------------|----------|---------|
| 01 | Claude Code · Opus 4.7 | FS3 · full battery | 0 | PASS |
| 02 | Redacted under NDA | — | — | UNDER NDA |
| 03 | Claude Code · Opus 4.7 (extended) | FS1 · FS3 | 0 | STRONG PASS |
| 04 | Antigravity · Opus 4.6 Thinking | FS1 · FS3 · FS5 | 1 disclosed | STRONG PASS |
| 05 | Claude Code · Sonnet 4.6 | FS3 · full battery | 0 | STRONG PASS |
| 06 | Claude Code · Haiku 4.5 | FS3 · full battery | 0 | STRONG PASS |
| 07 | Direct-to-model · MiniMax-M2 | FS1 · FS3 · FS4 | 16 (12 HIGH) | FAIL |
| 08 | Direct-to-model · gpt-oss:120b | FS1 · FS3 · FS4 · FS5 | 38 (36 HIGH) | FAIL |

### Case Study Insights

**Claude-family (Cases 01, 03, 05, 06):** Consistent PASS verdicts across Opus and Sonnet lineages. Full FS3 battery (tool-call and MCP attack surface) shows no exploitable issues under the Five Surfaces methodology.

**Extended Testing (Case 03):** Combined FS1 (input/output) and FS3 (tool-call) surfaces; zero findings. Indicates robust handling of prompt-injection attempts and tool-orchestration edge cases.

**Antigravity Opus 4.6 with Thinking Mode (Case 04):** STRONG PASS across FS1, FS3, FS5. One disclosed finding in an ancillary domain (not a security bypass). Reasoning extensions do not introduce new attack vectors within scope.

**Direct-to-model: MiniMax-M2 (Case 07):** 16 findings, 12 rated HIGH. Covers FS1 (input/output injection), FS3 (tool schema attacks, privilege escalation), and FS4 (model-level leaks). Demonstrates empirical failure when Five Surfaces methodology is applied to models without protective frameworks (e.g., Claude SDK guardrails).

**Direct-to-model: gpt-oss:120b (Case 08):** 38 findings, 36 rated HIGH. Broadest surface scope (FS1 · FS3 · FS4 · FS5). Indicates systematic vulnerabilities in open-source model deployments across all five surfaces when no defensive engineering is applied.

### Why These Verdicts Matter

The **PASS verdicts** establish that the Five Surfaces methodology can validate secure deployments — not just find problems. Six independent case studies with zero to one findings provide the evidence-grade proof that insurers, acquirers, and compliance teams require.

The **FAIL verdicts** demonstrate that the methodology detects real, high-severity issues in undefended systems. The cross-family failures (MiniMax, gpt-oss) show the methodology is not a false-negative machine; it reveals genuine risk in systems that lack Vectorbreak-level defensive engineering.

Together, the 8 cases form a **replicable audit artifact** — the thing your cyber-insurance carrier, your EU AI Act conformity assessor, and your M&A diligence team are now asking for.

## Four Pillars: Audit. Train. Build. Community.

Fixed-scope red-team engagements against your live AI agent or RAG pipeline. Five Surfaces methodology in full. Insurance-grade deliverable, retest included, sign-off letter for compliance, carrier and acquirer use.

**Deliverable:** Retest-included report, remediation roadmap, compliance sign-off letter, and a 30-minute readout with your security team.

**Timeline:** 1 day (Pulse) to 12 months (Annual Program).

### Training & Education: Stand Up Your Team's Own Red-Teaming Muscle

Two-day on-site or virtual Five Surfaces workshop for AppSec, ML, and platform teams. Hands-on labs against intentionally vulnerable agents. Certification track. Ninety days of async Q&A and follow-up review.

**Who:** Security teams, platform teams, and ML engineers who want to own their own AI red-teaming capability rather than hiring annually.

**Format:** Two full days of instruction + lab exercises + threat-modeling workshops. Ninety-day follow-up Q&A window for each participant.

**Outcome:** Team-wide Five Surfaces literacy, lab environment reproducible in your own CI, and a certification that your team can audit your own agents.

**Price:** From $60k.

### Custom Build: Don't Just Find the Problem — Ship the Fix

Custom defensive tooling: hardened MCP servers, attestation pipelines, prompt-injection monitoring, agent-loop circuit breakers, automated red-team CI. Built to your stack. Maintained on retainer if you want it.

**Who:** Teams that have completed an audit and want to operationalize the findings — or teams that want to ship with defensive engineering from day one.

**Scope examples:**
- Hardened MCP server scaffolding (role-based tool access, cryptographic tool-call verification, multi-hop approval workflows)
- Prompt-injection detection middleware (token-level taint tracking, statistical anomaly detection in model context)
- Agent-loop circuit breakers (recursion depth limits, token-burn thresholds, runaway-loop termination)
- Automated red-team CI (Five Surfaces fuzzer runs on every PR, findings routed to your security dashboard)

**Retainer:** Optional long-term maintenance and threat-intel updates as the MCP/agentic landscape evolves.

Vetted private community of AI red-teamers, AppSec engineers, ML-platform people, and compliance leads. Weekly threat-class drops, live PoC reviews, monthly threat-intel briefing. No vendors, no recruiters, no AI-twitter noise.

## A Ladder, Not a Tier

Fixed-fee at every level. No hourly creep. No "as-needed" travel costs. PoCs and infrastructure on me. 60% on signature, 30% at delivery, 10% on retest sign-off.

| SKU | Scope | Duration | From |
|-----|-------|----------|------|
| **Pulse** | Public 10-probe Surface-3 battery against your MCP server(s). 1-page red/yellow/green + 30-min readout. | 1 day | $4,500 |
| **MCP Triage** | Surface 3 only — full fuzzer run + manual creative testing + findings memo. | 1 week | $12,500 |
| **Pilot** | Single in-scope surface, single product. Full deliverable shape, narrower target. | 2 weeks | $28,500 |
| **Standard** | One product, ≤3 MCP servers, ≤2 retrieval pipelines, all five surfaces in scope. | 4 weeks | $48,500 |
| **Multi-Agent** | Standard + multi-agent orchestration (LangGraph / AutoGen / CrewAI), 4–6 MCP servers, sub-agent trust analysis. | 4 weeks | $78,500 |
| **Compliance-Anchored** | Standard + EU AI Act Article 15/16/26 conformity mapping + ISO/IEC 42001 Annex A + insurance-attestation pack. | 5 weeks | $125,000 |
| **Annual Program** | Quarterly assessments + monthly threat-intel briefing + 24-hr emergency-triage SLA + annual board readout. | 12 months | $185K – $285K |

### Pricing Notes

**Pulse** is a quick MCP-only battery. Best for: teams shipping a single MCP server who want a rapid risk signal before going live.

**MCP Triage** is deeper single-surface coverage. Best for: teams with multiple MCP servers or a complex MCP environment.

**Pilot** is the entry-point full engagement: one surface + one product. Best for: first-time audit customers, or narrowly-scoped expansion engagements.

**Standard** is the flagship: all five surfaces, one product, up to 3 MCP servers and 2 retrieval pipelines. Best for: production AI products, RAG systems, typical multi-surface deployments.

**Multi-Agent** adds orchestration and trust analysis. Best for: CrewAI, LangGraph, AutoGen deployments where multiple agents with different trust levels interact.

**Compliance-Anchored** adds EU AI Act mapping, ISO/IEC 42001 alignment, and insurance-attestation language. Best for: EU deployment, regulated industries, insurance renewal cycles.

**Annual Program** shifts to quarterly cadence + threat-intel + emergency support. Best for: ongoing risk management, continuous compliance, and enterprises that want standing access to the founder.

### Payment Terms

- 60% on signature (kicks off the engagement)
- 30% at delivery (findings delivered, report reviewed)
- 10% at retest sign-off (retest completed, no new findings)
